newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Balkans tense despite calm in Serbia, Bulgaria.
newsitem.headline: Balkans tense despite calm in Serbia, Bulgaria.

text.p: Bulgaria and Serbia have averted crises which threatened to turn increasingly violent, but in Albania and Greece protesters and riot police faced off again on Thursday, keeping the Balkans tense and unpredictable.

Albania, Europe's poorest state, has emerged as the most dangerous troublespot with protesters taking to the streets repeatedly to challenge the rightwing government over failed get-rich-quick investment schemes.

"In Greece and Bulgaria, the problems are largely economic, in Serbia, they are largely political but in Albania, they are both," said analyst Kancho Stoychev, director of the Gallup International polling company in Sofia.

In Vlore, southern Albania, some 30,000 protesters, blaming President Sali Berisha for the collapse of investment schemes, swept by riot police to occupy the city centre in a second day of protests on Thursday.
"Vlore is ours, down with the government!" the crowd chanted, demanding the resignation of Berisha's government. "Sali, you thief, where have you put our money," they yelled.
Three demonstrators and three policemen were injured in clashes on Wednesday when security forces used water cannon and dogs, and shots rang out periodically.
Berisha has tried since January to halt the protests with a mixture of pledges of partial repayments of hundreds of millions of dollars and a tough police clampdown on dissent.
"Berisha may be sitting on a time-bomb. If, as many think, the collapse goes further than we have seen, then this will be back to haunt him," said one diplomat in Sofia.
Berisha won elections last May, which observers said were fraudulent. But opposition parties have been unable so far to organise an effective common front against him.
Bulgaria and Serbia pulled back this week from the brink of all-out confrontation between ruling ex-communists and anti-government demonstrators.
In Serbia, thousands of protesters have rallied daily for 11 weeks to protest against election fraud and complain about autocratic leader Slobodan Milosevic.

Milosevic, blamed for fueling the ethnic wars which tore Yugoslavia apart in 1991, caved in and agreed to reinstate the election results two days after he ordered police out against the protesters -- threatening to provoke widespread violence.
Serbian opposition leaders said they would end their street protests if parliament approved a bill next Tuesday to reinstate their November municipal election victories in 14 towns.
Bulgaria's ruling Socialists stepped back from open conflict with anti-government protesters this week, resigning and calling elections nearly two years early.
"From the political point of view, Serbia is still very dangerous but from the economic point of view Bulgaria is very dangerous," Stoychev said.

Opposition leader Ivan Kostov's Union of Democratic Forces, which staged 30 days of mass protests to force the Socialists out, is favoured to win elections in April and secure a strong mandate to implement urgently need economic reforms.
But in the meantime the economy is sinking further by the day, with hyperinflation, a shattered banking system and the lev, the national currency, in collapse.
Food prices have soared, causing alarm among Bulgarians, and many petrol stations have closed for lack of fuel.
Economic turmoil in Bulgaria and Albania threatens to cause problems for neighbouring Greece if illegal immigrants flood over the border to find work.

Greece, the only Balkan country in the European Union and NATO alliance, already has problems of its own. The socialist government of Costas Simitis has imposed tough measures to prepare the EU's poorest state for monetary union by 2001.
That has triggered recent widespread protests and strikes by civil servants, teachers, workers, diplomats, seamen and others who fear a sharp drop in their standard of living.
Thousands of farmers and riot police faced off this week, with the farmers threatening to seize road and rail links again to press their economic demands.
They stopped virtually all road and rail traffic for 25 days in December and Simitis has been hard pressed to find a way to tame them.
He sent helicopters and 5,000 police to the farm region. They have chased the farmers around for two days but farmers say they can block road and rail links any time they want.
